source: Zhong et al. (2023) MemoryBank: Enhancing LLMs with Long-Term Memory
finding: First widely cited LLM memory with a forgetting curve. Retention R = exp(-t/S). S starts at 1 and goes up by 1 each time the memory is recalled, and t resets to 0. So recall (a proxy for use) protects a memory.
numbers: 194 probing questions (97 English, 97 Chinese). SiliconFriend with ChatGPT: retrieval accuracy 0.763 (EN) and 0.711 (ZH); correctness 0.716 and 0.655; coherence 0.912 and 0.675. ChatGLM retrieval 0.809 / 0.84; BELLE 0.814 / 0.856.
limits: Authors call it exploratory and highly simplified. No ablation of the forgetting rule, so the numbers do not show forgetting helps. Simulated users played by ChatGPT. Strength tracks past use, not predicted future use.
agent_relevance: Cheapest relevance proxy: count how often a lesson was actually retrieved and used, and let unused lessons decay. Benefit untested.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
finding: Retrieval score = recency (exponential decay, factor 0.995 per game hour) + importance (LLM rates 1 to 10) + relevance (cosine similarity), each min-max scaled to [0,1]. Nothing is deleted; low-scored memories just do not surface. Reflection fires when summed importance of recent events passes 150 (about 2 to 3 times a day).
numbers: 100 Prolific raters ranked 5 conditions. TrueSkill: full 29.89 (sigma 0.72); no reflection 26.88; no reflection or planning 25.64; crowdworker 22.95; no memory, planning, reflection 21.21. Full vs prior-work baseline Cohen d = 8.16. Kruskal-Wallis chi2(4)=150.29, p<0.001.
limits: Ablations remove whole components, not the importance term alone. Believability judged by humans, not task success. Importance is rated at write time, so it is not true future relevance.
agent_relevance: Gives a ready write-time importance score plus a reflection trigger. Shows memory plus reflection beat no memory, but does not isolate the importance weight.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time
finding: Model reasons offline about a context before the query arrives, so it precomputes what a future query is likely to need. This is the computational version of consolidating what is expected to be asked. Same accuracy needs about 5x less test-time compute.
numbers: Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME. About 5x less test-time compute at equal accuracy. Scaling sleep-time compute adds up to +13% (GSM) and +18% (AIME). Multi-Query GSM-Symbolic: average cost per query down 2.5x at 10 queries per context. Models include gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, o1, o3-mini.
limits: Benefit shrinks when the query is hard to predict from the context. Gains are reported at matched test-time budgets. Stateful benchmarks were built by splitting a problem into context plus question.
agent_relevance: Supports an offline pass that precomputes for likely future needs. It also says where it works: when the future question is predictable.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute, section 5.4 predictability analysis
finding: Questions were binned in five quantiles by how predictable they are from the context (log-probability under Llama2-70B). The accuracy gap between sleep-time compute and plain test-time compute widened as predictability rose.
numbers: Stateful GSM8K-Symbolic P1 and P2, five predictability quantiles, Verbosity 0 prompt. Gap grows with predictability in both. Exact per-bin numbers are in a figure only.
limits: Predictability proxy is a language-model score, not a measured human relevance. Only math word problems.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM evidence that the value of pre-consolidation depends on expected future relevance. Use it to decide which lessons are worth building.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: Experience-Following Behavior
finding: Agents copy the output of the most similar stored task (experience-following). Two failure modes: error propagation (bad stored runs spread) and misaligned experience replay (stored runs that no longer fit the task). Deletion by past utility (history-based deletion) helps with a reliable utility judge.
numbers: Four agents: RegAgent, EHRAgent, AgentDriver, CIC-IoT. Strict evaluator, table read from layout: EHRAgent accuracy no-deletion 38.67 (1012 records), periodic 38.59 (302), history-based 42.06 (784), combined 42.34 (248). CIC-IoT 85.40 (904), 80.80 (310), 89.60 (788), 85.50 (188). RegAgent coarse: 63.18 no deletion (3511) vs 60.88 history-based (1012).
limits: Table columns are garbled in text extraction; the pairing above is my reading and should be checked against the PDF. History-based deletion with an unfine-tuned GPT-4o-mini judge helped EHRAgent but hurt AgentDriver. RegAgent lost accuracy with deletion.
agent_relevance: Closest direct test of dropping a lesson by expected future use: delete a record whose average utility across retrievals is low, only after it was retrieved more than n times. Needs a trustworthy utility signal.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents, selective addition
finding: Adding every run to memory (add-all) lets low-quality records pile up and performance fades over time. A strict gate on what gets stored helps. A coarse automatic gate behaves close to add-all.
numbers: Compared add-all, coarse automatic gate, strict human gate on the same four agents. Strict gate gives the best long-run results; exact numbers are in figures.
limits: The strict gate is a human oracle, so it is an upper bound, not something an agent has.
agent_relevance: Filtering at write time matters as much as pruning later. A weak self-judge is not a reliable gate.

source: Li and Li (2026) What Should an Agent Forget? RD-Forget
finding: Separates what is stored from what is used. Keep a source archive, and build a query-conditioned view per question. Superseded facts are suppressed for current-state questions and become eligible again for historical questions. A rate-distortion budget picks the view. Forgetting is local to the query.
numbers: Four models (Qwen3.5-flash, GPT-5.6-Luna, MiniMax-M2.5, Kimi-K2.5) and five suites. Three-suite means for RD-Forget: Qwen 66.59, Luna 86.71, MiniMax 77.13, Kimi 72.83. Ablation on Luna (matched full 91.86 AMB-Text, 93.59 LME-KU, 74.00 MAB-FC): remove forgetting 68.60/60.26/51.00; remove query conditioning 77.91/82.05/56.00. On BEAM: Qwen 50.21 vs ACE 32.84 and ReasoningBank 34.75.
limits: Compared against ACE and ReasoningBank under one answering pipeline. Small test slices (for example 150 BEAM questions). Preprint, not peer reviewed. Curator is a frozen LLM, so errors in relevance judgement carry through.
agent_relevance: Strong machine-side evidence for the reconciliation idea: keep the lesson, but gate its influence by the current problem. Do not delete; mark superseded, keep an archive.

source: Wei et al. (2026) FadeMem: Biologically-Inspired Forgetting for Efficient Agent Memory
finding: Two memory layers with different decay speeds. Decay rate depends on semantic relevance, access frequency and age. LLM resolves conflicts and fuses related items. Important memories decay 3 to 5 times slower than baseline; 23% of low-importance memories are promoted by access.
numbers: LTI-Bench after 30 days: critical facts retained 82.1% vs Mem0 78.4%, MemGPT 75.6%, LangChain 71.2%, Fixed-16K 50.2%; storage 55.0% vs 100% for Mem0. LoCoMo multi-hop F1 29.43 vs Mem0 28.37, MemGPT 9.46; factual consistency 85.9%; storage reduction 45%. MSC RP@10 77.2% vs 74.8% (Mem0). Ablation: no dual-layer 29.43 to 19.45 F1 (33.9% drop); no fusion 13.63 (53.7% drop); no conflict resolution 22.88 (22.4% drop).
limits: LTI-Bench is the authors' own. Gains over Mem0 are small (1 to 4 points). Preprint.
agent_relevance: A keep-or-fade policy based on relevance and use can cut storage about 45% with equal or better accuracy. Gains over a strong baseline are modest.

source: Xie (2026) Learning to Forget: SleepGate, sleep-inspired KV-cache consolidation for proactive interference
finding: Targets proactive interference: stale values in context disturb retrieval of current ones, falling log-linearly toward chance. SleepGate adds a conflict-aware tagger, a forgetting gate that evicts or compresses stale KV entries, and a consolidation module, run in sleep micro-cycles triggered by attention entropy.
numbers: Small transformer from scratch (4 layers, 793,344 parameters), synthetic PI benchmark. SleepGate 99.5% retrieval at PI depth 5 and 97.0% at depth 10. Five baselines (full cache, sliding window, H2O, StreamingLLM, decay-only) all below 18% at every depth. Theory: interference horizon from O(n) to O(log n) under assumptions.
limits: Proof of concept on a synthetic task with a tiny model trained for it. Not tested on real LLMs or real tasks. The decay-only baseline failing shows age alone is a bad forgetting signal there.
agent_relevance: Supports supersede, do not just age out: forgetting should key on conflicts with newer entries. Not a result about real agents yet.

source: Shinde (2026) SCM: Sleep-Consolidated Memory with Algorithmic Forgetting
finding: Architecture with working memory, multi-dimension importance tags, NREM and REM-style offline consolidation, and value-based forgetting.
numbers: Eight-test suite; perfect recall over ten-turn conversations; memory noise reduced by 90.9% by adaptive forgetting; search latency under 1 ms with hundreds of concepts.
limits: Self-described research preview and prototype. Ten-turn conversations are tiny. No external benchmark or baselines in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Low-weight evidence. Shows the design pattern exists; says nothing about real gains.

source: Kerestecioglu et al. (2026) Human-Inspired Memory Architecture for LLM Agents
finding: Six mechanisms: sleep-phase consolidation, interference-based forgetting, engram maturation, reconsolidation on retrieval, entity graph, hybrid retrieval. Thresholds were set on synthetic data, not on the benchmarks, to avoid leakage.
numbers: VSCode issues (13K issues, 120K events): dedup consolidation 97.2% retention precision, 58% store reduction, +21.8 points over baseline. LongMemEval M-tier streaming (475 sessions, 540K turns) at 200K-token budget: 70.1% vs 71.2% raw retrieval, overlapping 95% CI. S-tier (50 sessions): +13.3 points preference recall.
limits: Consolidation matched raw retrieval on LongMemEval, it did not beat it; the win is store size. Dedup, not relevance, drives the VSCode result. Only abstract and introduction read.
agent_relevance: Pruning the store roughly preserves accuracy at large scale. Do not expect accuracy gains from pruning alone.

source: Rusu, Khanzadeh and Alalfi (2026) Selective Forgetting: Graph-Based Memory for Long-Term LLM Agents
finding: Graph memory did not beat flat vector search, but pruning low-scoring nodes (weights on recency, access frequency, degree centrality, age) removed memory without hurting answers.
numbers: LongMemEval, 500 questions: graph token F1 0.417 vs flat 0.468, delta -0.050 (95% CI -0.085 to -0.016). Questions needing a specific prior assistant turn: judged correctness 0.911 down to 0.607. Pruning a 27,021-node graph removed 9.8% of nodes and 9.5% of bytes; token F1 +0.001 (CI -0.015 to +0.016); judged correctness -1.6 points (CI -3.8 to +0.6).
limits: Single small extractor model, one benchmark, one pruning pass. Authors say results describe this pipeline, not graph memory in general. Only about 10% pruned.
agent_relevance: A usage-and-centrality prune of about 10% was safe in this test. No evidence about deeper pruning.

source: Bering (2026) ZenBrain: 7-Layer Memory Architecture (principled-forgetting ablation)
finding: Ebbinghaus-style decay barely helps retrieval quality at moderate load. A NoDecay variant cost only P@5 0.002 (Wilcoxon p=0.043, |d|=0.015). So forgetting here buys efficiency, not accuracy.
numbers: LongMemEval-500: reaches 91.3% of a full-context oracle's binary-judge accuracy. Simulation-selection sleep loop: +37% stability and 47.4% storage reduction. Routing beats flat baseline by +20.7% F1 on LoCoMo.
limits: Author notes LoCoMo substring F1 favours lexical retrieval (BM25). One-author preprint; p=0.043 does not survive Bonferroni correction.
agent_relevance: Forgetting rarely improves accuracy by itself; it pays in cost and stability. Set expectations accordingly.

source: Bering (2026) ZenBrain: cooperative masking
finding: Under moderate load 14 of 15 ablations looked costless. Raising decay to 0.25/day over 60 days made 9 of 15 critical. Light-load tests underestimate how much memory mechanisms matter.
numbers: Quality Q down by as much as 93.7% in the stress setting (10 seeds, Wilcoxon); five mechanisms went from exactly 0% to below -89%. Moderate (0.15, 45 d), challenging (0.20, 50 d), stress (0.25, 60 d).
limits: Simulated memory pool, not real agent tasks.
agent_relevance: Test pruning rules under heavy load and long horizons, or null results will mislead.

source: Rana et al. (2026) OBLIVION: Self-Adaptive Agentic Memory Control through Decay-Driven Activation
finding: Forgetting as lower accessibility, not deletion. Read path: consult memory only when agent uncertainty and buffer utility call for it. Write path: reinforce only memories that contributed to the answer. Decayed items can be reactivated by cues.
numbers: Normalized score out of 10/11 per setting. Phi-4-mini at 120K: full context 1.15, BeyondPrompts memory 2.52, Oblivion 3.37. Qwen3-30B-A3B at 120K: 4.25 / 4.17 / 5.30 (full context / memory / Oblivion, first column read from layout). GPT-4.1-mini: 6.29 to 8.41 at 2K and 6.05 to 6.79 at 32K over full context. Token cost down 68% at 32K and up to 73% at 120K.
limits: Model-dependent margins. Reinforcement credit goes to memories contributing to the response, which the model judges itself.
agent_relevance: Matches the reconciliation: weak traces stay recoverable, strong traces rise by use. Good template for a decay-with-reactivation lesson store.

source: Yan et al. (2026) Memory-R1: RL-trained ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP memory manager
finding: A Memory Manager is trained with PPO or GRPO to choose ADD, UPDATE, DELETE or NOOP; an Answer Agent filters retrieved memories. Prompted managers often DELETE and ADD where an UPDATE was right, fragmenting memory.
numbers: Only 152 training QA pairs. Relative gains over the strongest baseline with GRPO: +28% F1, +34% BLEU-1, +30% LLM-as-a-Judge on LoCoMo; generalises to MSC and LongMemEval and to 3B to 14B models.
limits: Trained on one QA data source; reward is answer correctness, so the manager learns what helps question answering, not general future use. Heavy for a no-training scaffold.
agent_relevance: Outcome reward can teach what to keep. For a scaffold: log whether each memory edit helped later answers.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: Insight list with operators ADD, EDIT, UPVOTE, DOWNVOTE. Each insight has an importance count; it rises on UPVOTE or EDIT, falls on DOWNVOTE, and the insight is removed when it reaches zero. An agent-loop pruning rule by agreement over experience.
numbers: Benchmarks HotpotQA, ALFWorld, WebShop. Ablations: insights extracted only from the initial few-shot examples gave no gain over ReAct; success/failure pair comparison needed; adding reflections into insight extraction hurt; random in-context example choice dropped performance. Exact table cells not quoted (garbled in extraction).
limits: The removal rule was not ablated alone. Vote decisions are made by the same LLM.
agent_relevance: Ready-made lesson keep/drop rule: count votes against new evidence and remove at zero. Note reflections hurt.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Induces reusable workflows from successful past runs (offline, or online from runs judged correct) and keeps them in memory. Only judged-correct trajectories are kept.
numbers: WebArena: +51.1% relative success rate over the best autonomous method and +7.9% over a method with human-written workflows. Mind2Web cross-task: +24.6% relative step success.
limits: No removal of workflows. The keep rule relies on an evaluator.
agent_relevance: Another instance of keep only what worked; useful as a write-time filter.

source: Chhikara et al. (2025) Mem0: Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
finding: LLM extracts facts and then decides ADD, UPDATE, DELETE or NOOP against existing memory.
numbers: On LoCoMo: 26% relative gain in LLM-as-a-Judge over OpenAI memory; 91% lower p95 latency and over 90% token cost saving versus full context.
limits: Vendor authors; the gain is mostly cost; accuracy gain is relative to one baseline. Only abstract and intro read.
agent_relevance: Baseline CRUD loop that many pruning papers compare to.

source: Behrouz et al. (2026) Language Models Need Sleep
finding: Sleep paradigm for LLMs: consolidation by distillation (Knowledge Seeding) into a larger network, then Dreaming, where the model uses RL to build synthetic rehearsal data for new knowledge.
numbers: Reports gains on long-horizon, continual learning, knowledge incorporation and few-shot tasks; numbers not extracted.
limits: Weight-level method, not a scaffold. Only abstract and introduction read.
agent_relevance: Out of scope for a no-training agent; confirms the field's direction.

source: Gu et al. (2026) FSFM: Selective Forgetting Framework for Agent Memory
finding: Taxonomy of forgetting: passive decay, active deletion, safety-triggered, adaptive reinforcement. Claims value from efficiency, memory quality and safety.
numbers: Controlled experiments: access efficiency +8.49%, signal-to-noise +29.2%, 100% elimination of security risks (as stated).
limits: Mostly a design and position paper; the setup behind the numbers is thin, and 100% is on the authors' own test. Only abstract and introduction read.
agent_relevance: Low weight; useful as a list of reasons to forget: cost, quality, safety.

source: Liu et al. (2026) DREAM: Forgetting is Not Always Bad (poisoned agent memory)
finding: Training-free repair: weak reactivation destabilises a bad memory, anomalies are diagnosed, harmful ones suppressed and benign ones reinforced.
numbers: Attack success rate reduced by over 95% against backdoor poisoning; 92.96% task success in poisoned multi-agent systems.
limits: Security setting; relevance here means harmful, not useful later. Only abstract read.
agent_relevance: Forgetting also removes wrong lessons. Links to error propagation.

source: Feld and Born (2020) Neurochemical mechanisms for memory processing during sleep (Neuropsychopharmacology; online 2019)
finding: Two accounts of relevance: dopamine during sleep, or tagging during learning (favoured), where dopamine at encoding tags high-reward memories for preferential reactivation in later sleep. Replay may strengthen relevant and weaken irrelevant traces; ripple timing may set potentiation vs depression.
numbers: Cited, not new: telling people a word-pair list will be tested lets sleep help (ref 62); pramipexole removed the reward advantage but not the encoding-strength advantage; weakly encoded memories are replayed more and gain more from sleep.
limits: Review states reward effects are less consistent (negative, null and generalising results exist); direction of plasticity unclear; sulpiride follow-up was a preprint. First 100,000 characters of 222,299 read.
agent_relevance: Core source for the theory. The tag-at-encoding idea maps to scoring a lesson when it is written.

source: Kolibius, Born and Feld (2021) Vast amounts of encoded items nullify but do not reverse the effect of sleep on declarative memory
finding: Boundary condition: with 640 word pairs, sleep gave no benefit and also no extra forgetting. The earlier study found a sleep benefit at 160 pairs and none at 320.
numbers: N=78 (sleep 38, wake 40). Retention loss wake -11.2 (SEM 1.73) vs sleep -8.5 (SEM 1.70), F(1,74)=1.25, p=0.27. Equivalence test rules out a harm larger than d=-0.20 (p=0.02). BF01=8.26 against a harmful effect; positive effect inconclusive (BF01=1.45).
limits: Short retention interval; intentional encoding; did not test relevance directly.
agent_relevance: Consolidation has a capacity limit. Many lessons at once dilute offline processing; cap the batch.

source: Wilhelm et al. (2011) Sleep selectively enhances memory expected to be of future relevance
finding: Founding human result (as recalled and per its title): people who expected a later test kept more after sleep than those who did not. Not verified here.
numbers: Not read this session (page blocked); no numbers recorded.
limits: Details not verified. Later work (see the Feld and Born review) lists mixed reward and expectation results.
agent_relevance: Origin of expected future use as the keep signal.

source: Stickgold and Walker (2013) Sleep-dependent memory triage
finding: Review arguing sleep triages memories by emotional salience and expected relevance rather than consolidating everything (from title only).
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Not opened; cited from the Europe PMC record only.
agent_relevance: Alternate theory source for the keep/drop idea.

source: Search note: no study found that tests relevance-based memory fate in LLM agents with a human-style design
finding: Across the 2023 to 2026 papers found, relevance means a proxy: retrieval count, LLM importance rating, query match, recency. No paper tests whether predicted future relevance made at write time beats a rule using past use. Closest tests: history-based deletion, RD-Forget query-conditioned view, sleep-time compute predictability analysis.
numbers: Search coverage limited: web search quota was spent; used arXiv listing search and Europe PMC only.
limits: Absence of evidence in a partial search.
agent_relevance: Treat relevance-based pruning as untested. Compare write-time prediction against use-count in our own harness.
